_help: Capstones. capstones[] -> {code, name, pre[] (must exist in courses.json), pre_want[] (used only if the course exists), blurb, hours, brief[], phases[{t, items[], links[{t,h}]}], rubric[], extras?}. Each item is a checkbox; the capstone is complete when every item is ticked. Item key = CODE.<flat index>, so never reorder items without accepting that saved ticks shift. Progress lives in localStorage oxday-courses under 'cap'.

capstones.name: Blue capstone: investigate a breach
capstones.blurb: Work a full simulated intrusion from the raw evidence to a written incident report.
brief: You are the on-call analyst at a fictional company, Brightwater Logistics. At 12:09 UTC the SOC isolated a file server after a ransomware precursor fired. Your job is to find out how the attacker got in, what they touched, what left the network, and what to change so it does not happen again.

The evidence is a case file of email, proxy, endpoint, authentication, DNS and firewall logs. Everything in it is invented and uses reserved example domains and documentation IP ranges. Work it like a real ticket: build a timeline first, form hypotheses, and only then write conclusions.
Do the investigation before opening the answer key at the bottom of the case file. The report is the deliverable, not the answers.

items: Read the whole case file once without taking notes, then list every host, account and external address that appears
Write a one-paragraph problem statement: what was detected, when, and what you are trying to prove
Pick a timestamp convention (UTC) and record it at the top of your timeline
Merge every log source into one timeline sorted by time, one line per event, with the source named
Mark the first malicious event (initial access) and the last one you can see
Identify patient zero: the first host and account that were compromised
Calculate dwell time from initial access to containment
Explain the initial access vector and show the evidence for it
Identify the command-and-control infrastructure (domains and IPs) and the beacon interval
Show how credentials were stolen and which account was abused afterwards
Trace lateral movement hop by hop, naming the protocol used for each
Identify persistence on any host
Quantify data exfiltration: destination, volume, and which host it came from
Describe the impact that was attempted and whether it succeeded
Map each stage of the attack to a MITRE ATT&CK technique ID
Write an indicator list (domains, IPs, file names, hashes, service names) in a table
Write at least two detection ideas: one log query or rule that would have fired earlier
Executive summary a non-technical manager can read in two minutes
Timeline table with times, hosts, events and evidence source
Root cause and contributing factors
Impact assessment: systems, accounts and data affected
Containment, eradication and recovery steps, in order
Recommendations ranked by effort and payoff
Lessons learned: what worked, what was missing, what to rehearse
Compare your findings with the answer key and note anything you missed or got wrong

rubric: A reader who was not there could follow the attack from your report alone
Every claim points at a specific log line
Timeline is in UTC and sorted
Findings and recommendations are separate sections
You say what you do not know instead of guessing

capstones.name: Red capstone: attack the homelab
capstones.blurb: Run a scoped penetration test against your own lab, then write the findings the way a client would receive them.
brief: Test your own homelab as if you were a hired tester. The point is the method and the paperwork: scope, rules of engagement, notes, evidence, a ranked findings report, and a retest after fixes.

Only attack systems you own and have written down as in scope. Do it on an isolated lab network or a snapshot you can roll back, never on shared school, work or home networks other people rely on. Take a snapshot of every VM first.
Hardening is part of the job. Every finding gets a fix, and you retest to prove the fix worked.

items: Write the scope: exact hosts, IP ranges and what is off limits (router, anything holding real data, other people's devices)
Write the rules of engagement: test window, allowed techniques, no denial of service, stop conditions
Snapshot every in-scope VM and confirm you can roll back
Draw the network diagram you are about to test and keep it with the report
Discover live hosts and open ports; save the raw scan output
Fingerprint services and versions, then list candidate weaknesses per service
Enumerate users, shares and web content where applicable
Write a one-page attack plan ranking targets by likely payoff
Get an initial foothold on at least one host and record every step
Attack a web application in the lab (for example DVWA or WebGoat) and document at least two vulnerability classes
Crack or reuse at least one credential using a method you can explain
Escalate privileges on a host, or explain precisely why you could not
Attempt movement to a second host, or to Active Directory if the lab has one
Find your own activity in the lab's logs or IDS and note what was and was not detected
Write one detection rule or alert for something that slipped through
Clean up: remove tools, accounts and persistence you added, or roll back the snapshots
Executive summary with an overall risk rating and the three things to fix first
Findings table: title, affected host, severity, evidence, impact, fix; one row per finding
Attack narrative that strings the findings into the path you actually took
Apply the fixes to at least three findings
Retest each fixed finding and record pass or fail with evidence
Add a lessons section: what you would test next time

rubric: Scope and rules of engagement were written before any scan was run
Each finding has reproducible steps and evidence
Severity ratings are justified, not guessed
Fixes are specific (setting, patch, rule), not 'improve security'

extras.title: Findings table skeleton
rows: Change password, restrict to management VLAN
extras.note: Example rows are placeholders to show the shape. Replace them with your own findings.

capstones.name: Build and publish a security tool
capstones.blurb: Ship a small, useful security tool to a public repo with tests, docs and a release.
brief: Build one small tool that solves a real problem you have run into, finish it, and publish it. Finished and small beats ambitious and half done. A recruiter reading your repo should understand what it does in thirty seconds.
Write it in a language you can defend in an interview (Python is a fine default). Do not commit secrets, real logs, or anything from a real employer or customer.

items: Choose an idea from the list below or your own, and write a one-sentence purpose
Write three user stories: who runs it, with what input, and what they get
Define done: the smallest version that is still useful, and what is explicitly out of scope
Create the repo with a license, a .gitignore and a README stub
Implement the core feature end to end before adding options
Validate all input and fail with clear error messages
Keep secrets and paths out of code; use arguments or environment variables
Commit in small steps with messages that say why
Write automated tests for the core logic and at least three bad-input cases
Run a linter or static analyzer and fix what it finds
Scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities and pin versions
Write a short threat model: what could an attacker do with your tool, and what do you do about it
README with purpose, install, usage examples with sample output, and limitations
A demo: a short GIF or pasted terminal session
Set up CI that runs the tests on every push
Tag a release with a changelog
Add the project to ~/projects and a bullet to your resume

rubric: It runs from a clean checkout following only the README
No secrets or personal data in the history
You can explain every design choice out loud

extras.title: Idea starters
list: Log parser that flags brute-force logins and prints a summary
Port and banner scanner with JSON output
File integrity checker that hashes a folder and reports changes
Password audit tool that checks a list against rules and a breach-hash file
Phishing header analyzer: SPF, DKIM, DMARC and mismatched domains
Sigma-style rule runner over JSON logs
IOC extractor that pulls IPs, domains and hashes out of text and de-duplicates them
Subnet and CIDR calculator with a study mode
